claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially a fully disordered high-temperature BCC phase without established chemical segregation.
Phase stability is governed by competition between a thermodynamic driving force for chemical ordering and kinetic limitations on atomic rearrangement.
B2 ordering occurs preferentially in Ni-Co-Al-rich regions, while Cr-Fe-rich regions form a disordered BCC solid solution.
Cr and Fe precipitate out of the B2 phase as its ordering increases.
The high-temperature BCC state is thermodynamically unstable toward B2 formation.
The tendency toward B2 ordering arises from stronger mutual affinities among selected constituent elements.
Rapid cooling suppresses diffusion and kinetically traps a metastable disordered BCC state.
Slow cooling or an isothermal hold permits diffusion-mediated segregation and enhances B2 ordering.
A temperature-dependent ordering or phase-separation change occurs in the approximate 600-800 °C regime.
Using identical initial microstructures allows cooling-dependent kinetic effects to be isolated.
Slow-cooled or isothermally held specimens will have a higher B2 phase fraction than rapidly quenched specimens.
Rapidly quenched specimens will retain predominantly disordered BCC structure.
An intermediate cooling rate produces a mixed microstructure.
Ordered and disordered BCC phases can coexist in Al-containing Cr-Fe-Ni-based multicomponent alloys.
The proposed mechanism may cease to apply when additional phases emerge or substantial initial compositional inhomogeneity is present.
Quantitative phase fractions and the ordering-temperature window depend on diffusion coefficients and processing details.
Failure of the held or slow-cooled specimens to develop statistically more B2 than quenched specimens would falsify the proposed cooling-history mechanism.
Absence of Ni-Co-Al versus Cr-Fe chemical segregation would falsify the proposed segregation-mediated mechanism.
